power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.5", Sentence = "During training, we applied random horizontal flipping (p = 0.5) and random affine transformation (rotation ±10 •, translation ±5%, scaling 0.95-1.05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Schistosomiasis morbidity still persists in China despite extensive progress towards elimination of new and active infections.
Diagnosis of liver fibrosis related to Schistosoma japonicum remains challenging due to the subjective nature of ultrasound grading and the shortage of experienced sonographers in endemic counties.
Methods: We developed a deep learning model that grades schistosomal liver fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual delineation of a region of interest.
We used 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18-88 years, median age 54 years; 46.4% female) from a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023.
Of these, 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% had grade 0, 1, 2 and 3 fibrosis, respectively.

Fibrosis grades were based on the clinical ultrasound record and re-evaluation by an experienced radiologist according to the Chinese Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control; discordant cases were reviewed by a second radiologist and resolved by consensus.

Predictions from four neural networks with different architectures (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) were combined by weighted soft voting, with weights derived from validation performance.

Results: For the four-grade task this model achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184-0.8856), an accuracy of 0.8500 (0.8136-0.8818) and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (0.8983-0.9373) on a fixed test set of 440 images.
For detecting significant fibrosis (grade 2 or 3; test-set prevalence 0.530), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity was 0.9179, positive predictive value was 0.9300, negative 1.
Schistosomiasis-related morbidity persists in China despite substantial progress towards transmission interruption and the marked decline in active infections.
Schistosomiasis affects more than 250 million people worldwide, while Schistosoma japonicum is endemic mainly in China and the Philippines, with small residual foci in Indonesia.
Compared with other major human schistosomes, Schistosoma japonicum has substantially greater fecundity, resulting in a high tissue egg burden and potentially severe hepatosplenic morbidity [1].

text.text: Chronic infection can progress to hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension and, in severe cases, to advanced schistosomiasis with massive splenomegaly, ascites, colonic proliferative lesions, severe growth retardation or gastroesophageal variceal bleeding [2].

text.text: As China moves towards schistosomiasis elimination and active infections become increasingly rare, residual morbidity is becoming concentrated among previously infected populations [3] [4] [5].

text.text: Two-dimensional grey-scale (B-mode) ultrasonography is non-invasive, repeatable and widely available, and can visualise the characteristic hepatic changes of schistosomiasis japonica.

A distinctive feature is interseptal fibrosis, in which fibrous septa between hepatic lobules appear as echogenic bands outlining polygonal areas and producing a characteristic fishscale or network pattern.
Under the Chinese ultrasound grading scheme used in endemic areas, hepatic fibrosis is classified from grade 0 to 3.

Grade 0 represents a normal liver; grade 1 is characterised by scattered focal echodense areas and mildly coarsened echoes; grade 2 by stronger echogenic bands forming a fish-scale or fine network pattern; and grade 3 by a coarse, contiguous echogenic network, often accompanied by more extensive parenchymal and portal abnormalities [9].

text.text: These grades represent a continuum of increasing echogenicity, coarsening and network formation rather than categories separated by a single discrete feature.
Visual grading is therefore inherently observer-dependent, particularly at the boundaries between adjacent grades [9, 10].

text.text: In 2025 the National Institute of Parasitic Diseases convened more than 30 Chinese and international experts to publish an expert consensus on the ultrasound diagnostic pathway for this condition [9].

text.text: That consensus explicitly identifies artificial intelligence-assisted image recognition, grading and follow-up monitoring as an important direction for the field.
It is aligned with the WHO(World Health Organization) framework for verifying interruption of transmission and for post-interruption surveillance [9].

text.text: Artificial intelligence applied to ultrasound imaging has begun to show promise for automated assessment of schistosomal liver fibrosis.

Guo et al. extracted 851 radiomic features from manually delineated regions of interest and trained support vector machines, achieving validation AUCs of 0.771-0.834 for discrimination between adjacent grades [11]; this approach requires manual delineation before feature extraction and formulates grading as six pairwise tasks rather than a single four-grade prediction.

text.text: We therefore asked whether the four national grades could be predicted from a single B-mode image, without manual region-of-interest delineation, using images from one county hospital in Jiangxi Province, China (2,921 patients, one image each, 2019-2023).

Because the number of images was small by the standards of deep learning, we combined four backbones from different architectural families (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) by weighted soft voting rather than enlarging a single network, with weights determined exclusively from validation-set performance before evaluation on the held-out test set.
We also asked where the gain of the ensemble comes from, and report an activation map for each backbone so that the image evidence behind a prediction is available to the reading clinician.
This was a retrospective analysis of abdominal ultrasound images acquired at the Second People's Hospital of Duchang County, Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023.
Jiangxi Province is a major schistosomiasis-endemic area of China, and residents of the Poyang Lake region are at risk of exposure to infested water.
The hospital is the designated local hospital for schistosomiasis diagnosis and treatment.

Schistosomiasis was diagnosed according to the national Diagnostic Criteria for Schistosomiasis (WS 261-2006) [15], and Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis was graded with reference to the Handbook of Schistosomiasis Control [16].

text.text: The inclusion criteria were evidence of current or previous Schistosoma japonicum infection, defined as a documented history of schistosomiasis, a positive serological test for anti-Schistosoma japonicum antibodies, or a positive parasitological stool examination for S. japonicum, together with availability of right subcostal and right subcostal oblique ultrasound images.

Cases with conditions that could affect ultrasound assessment, such as fatty liver, hepatitis, or drug-or alcohol-induced liver injury, were excluded, as were images with severe distortion or poor quality.
Images were acquired with a Philips EPIQ 5 ultrasound system and a C5-1 convex-array transducer at 3.5-5.0 MHz, exported in DICOM format and de-identified before modelling.
The ultrasound grade recorded in the medical record was retrieved, and a radiologist with more than 5 years of experience in schistosomiasis ultrasonography re-evaluated each image.
A second radiologist reviewed cases with discordant grades, and disputed cases were discussed to decide on inclusion and final grade.
The final consensus labels were used for model training and defined a four-class task: schistosomal liver fibrosis grades 0, 1, 2 and 3 (G0-G3).
The grades are distinguished by the coarseness and spatial organisation of the parenchymal echo.
Grade 0 shows a uniform liver parenchymal echo with fine or slightly thicker bright spots.
In grade 1 the parenchymal echo is uneven and the bright spots become coarser.
In grade 2 the echo is unevenly distributed with enhanced bright spots that form a fish-scale pattern, and a fine mesh-like echo is seen throughout the liver [11].

text.text: In grade 3 the echo is uneven with thicker, more intense bright spots and higher-pitched echoes, and the echoes form a densely packed, coarse network-like highecho band [11].

text.text: This study was reviewed and approved by the Ethical Review Committee of the National Institute of Parasitic Diseases, Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention (approval no.
All participants were informed of the study's aims, procedures, potential benefits and risks before enrolment, and each provided written informed consent; no minors were enrolled.
The present analysis was performed retrospectively on de-identified ultrasound images, with no additional intervention or contact with participants.
The 2,921 included images, with one image per patient, were split into training, validation and test sets at a ratio of approximately 70:15:15, stratified by fibrosis grade using a random seed of 42.
Once defined, the training, validation and test sets were kept fixed throughout model development, with the test set held out and used only for the final evaluation.
The proportion of each fibrosis grade differed by no more than 0.47 percentage points across the three subsets (Fig. 1a).

text.text: Images were stored in Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) format as singlechannel grey-scale arrays of 360 × 385 pixels.
Each image was linearly stretched to 0-255 using its own minimum and maximum grey levels and resized to 224 × 224 pixels by bilinear interpolation.
It was then converted to a tensor and normalised with a mean of 0.5 and a standard deviation of 0.5.
Per-image stretching was intended to make the model rely on the relative grey-level distribution rather than on absolute echogenicity and thus reduce the effect of different gain settings.
During training, we applied random horizontal flipping (p = 0.5) and random affine transformation (rotation ±10 • , translation ±5%, scaling 0.95-1.05).
No augmentation was applied during validation or testing.
Models were trained and evaluated on a single workstation with a 20-core Arm CPU and one NVIDIA GB10 accelerator sharing 120 GB of unified memory (Linux kernel 6.17, NVIDIA driver 580.142).
The implementation used Python 3.12.3 with PyTorch 2.11.0 and torchvision 0.26.0 built against CUDA 13.0; metrics were computed with scikit-learn and activation maps with the grad-cam package.
All package versions are recorded in Supplemental materials.

We chose four backbones from different architectural families: ResNet-18 (residual convolutional network), EfficientNet-B0 (compound-scaled convolutional network with channel activation), DenseNet-121 (densely connected convolutional network) and Swin-T (hierarchical vision Transformer) [17] [18] [19] [20].

text.text: All four backbones were trained on identical data with an identical training procedure -loss function, optimiser, learning-rate schedule, augmentation and stopping rule -and differed only in architecture.

Each was initialised from ImageNet-1K pre-trained weights; the first convolutional (or patch-embedding) layer was adapted to single-channel input by averaging its pre-trained RGB kernels, and the whole network was then fine-tuned [23].

text.text: The loss was class-weighted cross-entropy with label smoothing [24] (coefficient 0.05), the weight of each class being proportional to the inverse of its training-sample count and normalised to sum to the number of classes.

text.text: The batch size was 32, gradients were clipped to a global norm of 1.0, and training ran for up to 30 epochs.
Training stopped early if the validation macro-F1 did not improve for 8 consecutive epochs, and the weights with the highest validation macro-F1 were retained as the final model.
The random seed was fixed at 42, with cuDNN deterministic mode enabled and benchmarking disabled to improve run-to-run consistency.
Ensembling was performed at the probability level.

Each backbone produced predicted class probabilities for the four grades; these were combined linearly with weights fixed before any test-set evaluation, and the grade with the highest combined probability was the final prediction: P (g) = 󰁓 a w a •P a (g).
The weights were the normalised best validation macro-F1 of each backbone, w a = F1 a / 󰁓 b F1 b : 0.2453 for ResNet-18, 0.2525 for EfficientNet-B0, 0.2480 for DenseNet-121 and 0.2542 for Swin-T.
No test data were used to estimate the weights.
Unlike majority voting, probability weighting preserves each model's uncertainty across grades, which suits a four-grade task in which adjacent grades are easily confused.
The primary metric was the macro-averaged F1 score (macro-F1).

Secondary metrics were accuracy, quadratically weighted kappa (QWK), mean absolute error (MAE) and, for the binary task of significant fibrosis (grade ≥2), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity and specificity.
On the fixed test set (n = 440), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated by non-parametric bootstrap with 1,000 resamples (random seed 42).
Models were compared by paired bootstrap, in which the same resampling indices were applied to the predictions of each model and to the reference labels.
Stability was assessed by five-fold cross-validation.
Grad-CAM (gradient-weighted class activation mapping) was computed for all four backbones on their final spatial feature layer.
For ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0 and DenseNet-121, Grad-CAM was applied to the final convolutional feature maps.
For Swin-T, the output of the second layer normalisation in the final transformer block was reshaped from 49 spatial tokens to its native 7 × 7 grid before Grad-CAM computation.
For all backbones, the target class was the grade predicted by the ensemble so that the resulting maps referred to the same class for a given image.
Maps were upsampled to 224 × 224 pixels, smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1.5), and normalised to [0, 1] within each image.
We then calculated the equal-weighted mean activation, the population standard deviation across the four maps, and the number of backbones with normalised activation above 0.5 at each pixel.
The diversity index was defined as the image-wide mean of the standard-deviation map, and the agreement ratio as the proportion of pixels at which all four backbones exceeded 0.5.

For the two intermediate grades, errors went in both directions but more often upwards: of the 27 G1 errors, 17 were graded G2 and 10 were graded G0, and of the 23 G2 errors, 16 were graded G3 and 7 were graded G1.

Among the single models, EfficientNet-B0 had the highest F1 for G0 (0.842) and G1 (0.836), ResNet-18 for G2 (0.788) and Swin-T for G3 (0.836).
The ensemble had the highest F1 in all four grades (0.862, 0.861, 0.828 and 0.860).

PPV varied more than NPV, spanning 0.699 to 0.919 against 0.855 to 0.986.
Across the table, a high PPV went with a low sensitivity rather than a high one (r = -0.51, P = 0.02), the expected trade-off between assigning a grade liberally and conservatively.
G1 shows this most clearly, with the highest mean PPV of any grade (0.889) and the lowest mean sensitivity (0.768).
The ensemble had the best PPV for G0, G2 and G3 and the best NPV for G2 and G3.
For G3 it combined a sensitivity of 0.889 with a PPV of 0.833, so advanced cases were largely detected and, when detected, usually correct.
These predictive values depend on the grade mix of the test set (13% G0, 34% G1, 33% G2, 20% G3) and would differ in a population with another prevalence.
We also read the four-grade output as two clinical yes/no questions.

For any fibrosis (G1-G3 versus G0; 384 versus 56 images), the ensemble detected 97.4% of fibrotic images with a specificity of 89.3%  and an AUROC of 0.983; the single models ranged from 94.3% to 97.4% in sensitivity and from 82.1% to 91.1% in specificity.

To test whether these results depended on the particular training run, we repeated the entire pipeline with 15 training seeds on the same fixed split, changing only the random seed.
Ensemble macro-F1 was 0.848 ± 0.011 across seeds (range, 0.820-0.862).
The single backbones varied more, with seed-to-seed SDs from 0.014 to 0.020.
The ensemble exceeded the best single backbone in all 15 seeds, by 0.025 on average.
We also re-partitioned the whole pool of 2,921 images into five patient-level folds and retrained the four backbones and the ensemble in each fold (Methods).
Ensemble macro-F1 on the held-out folds was 0.832 ± 0.014, against 0.811 ± 0.011 for the best single backbone of each fold.
Because the folds re-partition the same pool of patients as the fixed split, this measures the stability of the pipeline rather than providing an independent validation.
Grad-CAM maps show where the evidence for a backbone's decision was concentrated.
We refer to them as activation maps.
We first asked whether the four backbones highlight the same part of an image.
For each image we took the hottest 10% of pixels in each map and measured the overlap between every pair of backbones.
Two regions of that size placed independently would overlap by 0.10; identical regions would give 1.
The observed medians were 0.25 to 0.51 across the six pairs.
We also measured the distance between the two maps' single hottest pixels.
This was a median of 41 to 68 pixels, or 18 to 30% of the frame width, against 114 pixels for two independently placed points.
The maps therefore overlap far more than chance without coinciding (Fig. 2).

text.text: The differences between maps are not an artefact of how the maps were produced.

The target layer of every backbone outputs a 7 × 7 grid for a 224 × 224 input (Methods), and all four maps were upsampled to the input size by the same operator and normalised the same way, so no backbone's map is coarser or smoother than another's by construction.
Nor is the ordering explained by map extent.
Swin-T does mark a smaller area, with the region above half of a map's own maximum covering 9% of the frame against 29% for ResNet-18.
The disagreement followed architecture.

text.text: Using 2,921 images, we trained four backbones of different architectural families and combined them by weighted soft voting into a single four-grade reader that takes the whole image as input, without manual delineation of a region of interest.

On the fixed test set the ensemble reached a macro-F1 of 0.853 (95% CI, 0.818-0.886), and its advantage over each backbone (0.046 to 0.055 in macro-F1) had a paired 95% confidence interval that excluded zero.
The advantage held in all 15 training seeds and five cross-validation folds, so it does not depend on one fortunate training run.
The ensemble also reduced the size of the errors.
In the reported run, every one of its errors was between adjacent grades, whereas each backbone misgraded 1 to 4 images by two grades or more.
Is the ensemble worth its cost, and how it could be deployed?
The ensemble improved macro-F1 significantly over the best single backbone, a gain that readers can weigh against the cost of running four networks.
Three considerations favour the ensemble in this application.
First, the gain is consistent: it appeared in every seed and in 8 of the 16 grade-by-backbone comparisons after correction for multiple testing, most reliably at G2.
Second, the ensemble reduced the errors that matter most clinically, those spanning two or more grades, in the reported run and in most seeds.
Third, and contrary to what the word ensemble suggests, the ensemble does not require a larger machine than a single network.

The reason is that the four backbones are independent and are combined only through their output probabilities, so they can be evaluated one after another, each loaded, run and released before the next.
Peak memory is then set by the largest member rather than by their sum.
We measured this on the deployed configuration, at the input size the pipeline uses.

Evaluated sequentially, the ensemble's peak accelerator memory was 131.4 MB, identical to that of Swin-T alone, its largest member, and below the 219.1 MB measured when all four were held in memory at once.

What the ensemble costs is time, not hardware: 163.3 ms per image on four CPU threads, against 80.4 ms for the slowest single backbone and 10.8 ms for the fastest, and 10.9 ms per image with all four resident on an NVIDIA GB10 accelerator.
The four deployed backbones total 49.7 million parameters, 1.8 times the 27.5 million of Swin-T alone and about twice the 23.5 million of a single ResNet-50 in the same configuration.
Because images are graded one at a time rather than in a real-time stream, a few hundred milliseconds is not a clinical constraint, and no additional class of hardware is needed.
Two deployment routes therefore follow from the same set of trained weights, and the choice between them is governed by data protection rather than by computing capacity.
In the first, a single backbone runs locally on the ultrasound workstation, so that no image leaves the department and no network connection is required.
On these data ResNet-18 had the highest macro-F1 among the single models, while EfficientNet-B0 offers the best balance of specificity and size, at 4.0 million parameters and 10.8 ms per image.
The cost is the ensemble gain reported above, and the loss of the reduction in errors spanning two or more grades.

In the second, the full ensemble runs on an institutional server, which keeps one auditable copy of the model, allows it to be updated and monitored centrally, and removes any dependence on the specification of the individual workstation.

This route requires images to be transmitted, so it is the more demanding of the two in terms of governance: it presupposes de-identification at source, an encrypted channel, and the data-protection approvals of the institutions involved.
Combining classifiers at the probability level reduces the errors that are specific to individual members while leaving shared errors untouched [22], and this is what we observed.

text.text: All 35 test images misgraded by every backbone were also misgraded by the ensemble; on these images the four posteriors agreed on a wrong grade and the reference grade received a mean probability of only 0.105, so averaging could not recover it.

The gain came entirely from the images on which the backbones disagreed: in 24 of them, two or three backbones were wrong and the ensemble was right, either because a confident minority outweighed a less confident majority or because the errors fell on different grades and the reference grade had the highest probability after averaging.

For this mechanism to work, the members must err on different images, and members of different architectural families are the natural candidates, because convolutional networks and vision transformers are known to build different internal representations of the same image [21].

text.text: The activation maps were consistent with the observed prediction diversity.

Convolutional backbones showed more similar Grad-CAM patterns to one another than to Swin-T across all six similarity measures, indicating partly different spatial attribution patterns across architectures.

These differences may be related to the complementary prediction errors observed in the ensemble, but Grad-CAM alone cannot establish a causal link between attribution differences and ensemble performance.
Two lines of work are relevant.

Machine-learning readers for Schistosoma mansoni periportal fibrosis [12, 13] address a different pattern, the echogenic thickening along the portal tracts of the Niamey protocol, whereas S. japonicum produces a parenchymal network pattern graded by its coarseness and organisation [8, 9].

text.text: Theirs rests on the scale and the granularity of the labelled data, whereas ours asks how much can be obtained from 2,921 images acquired at a single centre.
That question led us to combine backbones of different architectural families rather than to enlarge a single one.
It also led us to report an activation map for every backbone, so that the image evidence on which a prediction rests is available to the reading clinician alongside the grade itself.
Their trained model is not released, and we did not attempt a direct comparison of the two.

Additionally, the study by Xu and colleagues required 18 ultrasound images per participant, whereas the present study requires only a single, relatively easy-to-acquire cross-sectional image of the liver.
This study has several limitations.
First, it was a single-centre retrospective study with a relatively homogeneous sample, and the external generalisability of the model has not been validated.

Second, only the clearest ultrasound image of each patient was included; information from multiple planes and time points was not used, and whether it could further improve grading remains to be evaluated.
Third, the model used grey-scale images alone, without clinical variables such as serology and medical history or multimodal information such as elastography.
Fourth, the study population was relatively old, with a mean age of 51.7 years, which may limit the generalisability of the model to younger populations.

This age distribution likely reflects the changing epidemiology of schistosomiasis in endemic areas, where new infections have declined substantially and most newly infected individuals recover after treatment, reducing the repeated infections that historically contributed to progression to advanced disease.
Future work will address these limitations along three lines.
A multicentre prospective validation study is ongoing to assess the stability and generalisability of the model across devices, populations and clinical settings.
Where necessary, federated learning may support joint modelling without sharing raw images.
We will also use multi-frame or multi-plane images as input and integrate clinical variables and elastography to enrich the information available to the model.
Finally, we will extend the model to longitudinal monitoring to track the progression or regression of fibrosis in individual patients.

A weighted soft-voting ensemble of four backbones graded Schistosoma japonicum-associated liver fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image on the four-grade scale, achieving a macro-F1 of 0.853 on the original test partition.
Its performance was higher than that of each individual backbone, and in the reported run all misclassifications were confined to adjacent grades.
The observed improvement was associated with complementary errors across the four architecturally different backbones.
For detecting grade ≥2 fibrosis, the ensemble achieved an AUROC of 0.982.
These findings support further evaluation of automated fibrosis grading in endemic settings, particularly through external and prospective validation.
